title: Primary Growth, Secondary Thickening, and Structural Support
objective: Distinguish length growth from stem thickening and connect both to plant loading and support.

terms.definition: Lengthening produced mainly by apical meristems.
Increase in stem or root thickness produced by lateral meristems.
Deposition of lignin that contributes rigidity and water-conducting tissue properties.
Growth change caused by mechanical stimulation such as movement or touch.

coreScience: Primary growth extends shoots and roots and adds new nodes, leaves, and branches. Secondary growth increases the diameter and transport capacity of established axes. Cannabis is herbaceous, but older stems can develop substantial secondary vascular tissue and strengthening as the plant becomes larger.

Mechanical loading can alter plant growth and structural allocation through thigmomorphogenesis, but wind also changes leaf microclimate, boundary layers, transpiration, and water stress. Results from touch, brushing, or another species cannot be converted into a universal cannabis fan setting. Violent airflow, repeated abrasion, constricting ties, and excessive training injury are damage risks rather than proven beneficial stress.

Structural failure occurs when load exceeds tissue or attachment strength. Flower mass, long lever arms, wet surfaces, wind, uneven canopies, narrow branch angles, and prior injuries all change risk. External support redistributes the load but does not correct a diseased or girdled stem.
cultivationRelevance: Install support before heavy loading makes placement destructive. Check ties regularly and allow for diameter expansion.
Measure both height and diameter when comparing architecture. Fast elongation without proportional thickening can increase lodging risk.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Stake, trellis, net, tie type, and installation date.
Air movement, outdoor wind, handling, and damage.
Location, load, weather or handling context, and corrective action.

misconceptions: A stronger fan always creates stronger stems: Excess air speed can cause injury, water stress, and distorted growth.
Silica or one additive guarantees branch strength: Structure is a whole-plant outcome and product claims require evidence.
Thick stems guarantee high yield: Stem diameter is one architectural trait, not a yield assay.
evidenceLimits: Cannabis-specific structural research is limited relative to general plant biomechanics. Treat support practices as risk management, not a proven potency or yield treatment.
